newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Access sees high Australian rate peak ahead.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Access sees high Australian rate peak ahead.

text.p: Australian interest rates will need to hit a higher peak than in previous economic recoveries to dampen an economy that will grow strongly in fiscal 1997/98, Access Economic said on Wednesday.

Access, in its March Economics Monitor publication, said growth would not pick up until the first half of 1997/98 (July-June), when recent interest rate cuts and strong housing and business investment would kick in.
"The economy is unlikely to really pick up pace until later in 1997, despite the U-turn in Reserve Bank rhetoric," Access said.
"Given the lags in interest rates working, the economy should show strong economic growth in 1997/98.
"Interest rates may need to rise by more in this recovery than in 1994/95 to dampen the economy."
Access said the chance of a fourth rate cut had now receded.
"The Reserve Bank appears to have sharply changed its rhetoric from viewing the glass as half empty to seeing it as half full," it said.
"Having just presided over a series of interest rate cuts, it claims that there are already signs of the economy picking up pace."
Access said the 1.5 percentage point cut in official rates in the final six months of calendar 1996 would accelerate the economic upturn in the fiscal year to June 30, 1998.
The economy would remain subdued in the final months of 1996/97, with full-time employment growth flat and a run-down in stocks.
The futures market also sees interest rates rising, with 90-day bank bills seen approaching eight percent by the end of calendar 1998.
In the last recovery, official rates rose 2.75 percentage points to peak at 7.5 percent in late calendar 1994.
Access said interest rate cuts now appeared to impact earlier than previously thought and continued to have a strong impact over 12 to 18 months.
"As a result, we expect strong economic growth over 1997/98 as housing joins business investment as the locomotives for economic activity," it said.
